guides.title: The first hour
guides.summary: Before you know how big this is — the actions that are right either way, and the one thing you cannot get back.
guides.text:
Something has stopped working and you don't yet know how big it is. The first hour is not for big decisions. It is for the handful of actions that are right whether this lasts three hours or three months, and for not doing anything you can't undo.
§ Stop, then look
• STOP — Stop, Think, Observe, Plan. Give it ten minutes before you drive anywhere or shout at anyone.
• Clear immediate hazards: fire, a smell of gas, water near live wiring, damaged structure. Deal with those or get out.
• Account for everyone in the house. Write down who is missing and where they should be.
• Treat injuries in order: catastrophic bleeding, then breathing, then everything else.
• Find out whether it is only you. Check the fuse box, then look down the street. A tripped breaker and a regional grid failure need completely different responses.
§ Fill everything with water
Mains pressure outlives the pumps by minutes to hours, and upper floors and high ground lose it first. This is the part of the hour you cannot get back.
• Fill the bath, buckets, pots, bottles, jerrycans, the kettle, the washing machine drum. Bath water is for washing and flushing, not drinking.
• A full bath holds roughly 150 litres (40 gallons). Your hot water cylinder holds another 150–190 litres (40–50 gallons) that you can drain off later.
• Cover what you fill. Anything open collects dust, insects and small hands.
§ Listen before you act
• Battery or wind-up radio, local AM/FM. Write down the time and what was actually said, not what you think it meant.
• If phones work, text rather than call — texts squeeze through congested networks when voice will not. One message: where you are, that you are safe, when you will next make contact.
• Charge every phone and power bank from whatever power you still have.
• Don't call emergency services unless it is an emergency. Every line you occupy is one somebody else needs.
§ Small, reversible, useful
• Keep the fridge and freezer shut from this moment. Every opening costs you hours of cold.
• Unplug sensitive electronics so a surge on restoration doesn't kill them. Leave one lamp switched on so you know the second power returns.
• If it's cold, choose one room now and start keeping the heat in it.
• If it plainly looks longer than a few hours and the roads are safe: fuel the car and draw cash. Both queues are unusable by hour three. If the roads are not safe, skip it.
• Start a written log — time, what you saw, what you did, what you decided. By day three you will not remember day one.
§ Don't
• Don't leave on a rumour, don't confront anyone, don't tell anybody what you have.
• Don't run a generator, camping stove, barbecue or charcoal indoors, in a garage, or in a tent. Carbon monoxide has no smell and kills people in their sleep.
• Don't take any decision in the first hour that you couldn't reverse in the second.

guides.title: The first 24 hours
guides.summary: Establish what happened, settle water and sanitation before they are urgent, and get everyone asleep.
guides.text:
By the end of the first day you want three things: a realistic idea of what has happened, water and a toilet arrangement that will hold for weeks, and everybody rested. Nothing else on this list matters as much as those.
§ Establish the facts
• Two listening sessions on the radio, not a radio left on all day. Note the source of everything you write down.
• Separate what you have seen from what you have been told. Rumour moves faster than news and is usually worse than reality.
• The questions that matter: how wide is it, is anyone coming, and what is the estimate for restoration. "No estimate" is itself an answer — plan for weeks.
§ Water
• Treat everything used for drinking, brushing teeth or washing food unless you are certain of the supply. Boil to a rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes above about 2,000 m / 6,500 ft), or use unscented household bleach at 2 drops per litre and wait 30 minutes.
• Plan on 3 litres per person per day for drinking alone, and about 15 litres a person a day for drinking, cooking and basic washing. Count your stored litres and divide.
• Don't ration drinking water. Dehydrated people make bad decisions. Ration washing, and go and find more water.
§ Sanitation — decide today
This is the decision that most determines whether your household is ill in three weeks. Make it while it is still theoretical.
• If the sewer still works and the drain runs, you can flush with 6–9 litres of grey water poured in fast. If the sewer is backed up, or you're downstream of a pumping station that has lost power, stop flushing immediately.
• Otherwise: two lined buckets today, one for urine, one for solids, with a cover material (sawdust, dry soil, shredded paper, wood ash) and a lid.
• Handwashing with soap at the point of use, from the first use. See the sanitation guide and take it seriously.
§ Food, warmth, people
• Eat the fridge today, the freezer over the next 48 hours, then dry stores. Cook meat that is thawing — cooked food keeps longer than raw, and a big cooked meal is morale.
• Heat or cool one room. Block draughts, get bedding into it, and put a battery carbon monoxide alarm in it if you are burning anything at all.
• Knock on your neighbours' doors, especially anyone old, alone or disabled. Two minutes each. It is the decent thing and it is also the single strongest thing you will do for your own security this week.
• Count medication in days, for every person. Anyone on insulin, oxygen or dialysis needs a plan tonight, while transport still works.
§ Communications and sleep
• Agree a household schedule: check-in times, an out-of-area contact everyone calls, a meeting point and a fallback. Write it on paper and give everyone a copy.
• Phones in flight mode, checked on a schedule. A phone at 5% is worth less than a phone at 40% tomorrow.
• Make the first go-or-stay assessment tonight, but don't act on it in the dark unless staying is dangerous.
• Then sleep. Split the night if you must, but nobody should be awake for 24 hours by choice. Exhausted people make the decisions that kill them.

guides.title: The first week
guides.summary: Stop reacting and start running a household — daily cycles, an honest inventory, and rationing set early.
guides.text:
Week one is the switch from emergency to routine. The adrenaline of day one is gone and the work is now repetitive: water in, waste out, food cooked, fuel gathered, people looked after. Build the systems while you are still strong and it is still light.
§ Turn each need into a daily cycle
• Water: a fixed route and time, containers that one person can actually carry (20 litres weighs 20 kg), a treatment step nobody skips, and separate storage for drinking and for washing. Never carry untreated water in the drinking containers.
• Sanitation: sited and built properly this week, not improvised for six months. Pit or trench at least 30 m (100 ft) from any well, spring or stream and downhill of it; covers on everything; handwashing at the point of use; a greywater soakaway away from the kitchen.
• Food: one cooking session a day if fuel is short. Cook once, eat twice.
• Fuel: gather ahead of use. Wet wood cut today is next month's fuel, not tonight's.
§ Inventory honestly
• Weigh and list the food. Actual weights, on paper, on the wall. Guessing at this stage compounds for months.
• Work out days of supply at about 2,000 kcal per person per day. People survive a long time on less, but below roughly 1,500 kcal work capacity falls off sharply and that is the thing you cannot afford.
• Do the same for water treatment, fuel, batteries, medication, soap, sanitation supplies. Write the run-out date next to each.
• Start rationing on day three to five — while it's a plan. Rationing that starts when the shelves are bare is panic, and it always cuts too hard, too late.
§ Name who owns what
Give every job a person: water, cooking, fuel, sanitation, watch, children, the sick, the log. Rotate the unpleasant ones. A household where everyone half-does everything does nothing well, and resentment starts inside a fortnight.
§ People, not just stores
• Turn the door-knocking into a network: who has a well, a generator, a chainsaw, medical training, a greenhouse, a spare room. Who lives alone. Who is frightened.
• Pool where it obviously pays — one cooking fire for three families burns a third of the fuel and makes a third of the smoke.
• Fix things now: the door, the broken window, the leaking gutter, the shelf. Repairs get harder as you get weaker.
§ Watch for illness
Diarrhoea in the household is a five-alarm event, not an inconvenience. Isolate the person, start oral rehydration solution (1 litre of clean water, 6 level teaspoons of sugar, half a level teaspoon of salt), disinfect surfaces with a 1:10 bleach solution, and find the cause: hands, water or food. It is almost always hands.
§ Then reassess
• Two fixed news windows a day. Write it down and turn it off.
• Revisit go-or-stay with a week of facts rather than day one's fear.
• If it is anywhere near the growing season, plant something. Radishes are up in 25 days, salad in 30. It costs an hour you still have.

guides.title: The first month
guides.summary: Do the arithmetic properly, fix the nutrition gaps, and turn neighbours into an organised community.
guides.text:
The first month is where optimism meets arithmetic. Consumption is now measurable, the novelty has gone, and whatever you improvised in week one either works or has quietly started to fail.
§ Recalculate against real consumption
• You now know what you actually burn, drink and eat per day. Redo every projection with those numbers, not the ones you assumed.
• Write the run-out dates somewhere everyone can see: food, cooking fuel, heating fuel, water treatment, batteries, each person's medication, soap, sanitary supplies.
• Start substituting before you are forced to. Stretch meals with grain and pulses. Keep one proper hot meal a day as a fixed point.
§ Nutrition, not just calories
Calories keep you alive; the rest keeps you working.
• Fat runs out first and is hardest to replace. Ration cooking oil harder than you want to.
• Protein: pulses, tinned fish, eggs, nuts. Weakness and slow-healing wounds are the early signs of running short.
• Vitamin C: deficiency shows at roughly one to three months without any — bleeding gums, old wounds reopening, exhaustion. Sprouted pulses, potatoes, fresh greens, rosehips and pine needle tea all supply it. Sprouting a jar of dried beans or lentils takes three days and no equipment.
• A daily multivitamin is trivial to store and covers most of this. Iodised salt covers another gap.
§ Fix what week one improvised
• Sanitation review: is the pit filling faster than expected, is soap still at the handwashing point, has anybody been ill and why.
• Maintenance: sharpen tools, sweep the flue (creosote is how houses burn down in month two), scrub water containers, repair boots.
• Health: look at the things nobody mentions — a tooth, a cut that isn't closing, weight loss, feet, a persistent cough. Weigh people if you have scales.
• Security: your routine is now set, which means it is predictable. Vary times. Walk outside after dark and look at your own house the way a stranger would.
§ Move from neighbours to community
• Organise what was ad hoc: shared cooking, shared childcare, a skills list, a notice board, a fixed market or meeting hour.
• Shared watch means everybody sleeps. Shared childcare frees the strongest labour. Shared meals cut fuel by more than half.
• Agree simple rules while everyone is still reasonable — how decisions get made, how disputes get settled, what happens to people who arrive.
§ Resupply and the season ahead
• Work out what can be legally scavenged, foraged, grown, fished, hunted or traded for. Find out what the local rules actually are; assuming they've lapsed is how people get hurt or arrested.
• Plan the next season now: winter fuel cut and stacked, spring seed set aside, storage prepared for a harvest you don't have yet.
• Get children into a structure of lessons and jobs. It is schooling and it is morale.
§ Expect the flatness
Month one is where adrenaline drains and the grey arrives — irritability, poor sleep, no appetite, nothing to look forward to. That is a normal response, not a failure. Structure, daylight, physical work and a fixed occasion each week are the treatment. See the morale guide.

guides.title: The first year
guides.summary: Stop consuming and start producing — food from the ground, fuel worked a year ahead, and skills that outlast stores.
guides.text:
A year in, stores are a memory and the question is whether you produce anything. The households that do well in the second year are the ones that spent the first making things other people need.
§ Calories have to come from somewhere
• A garden does not feed you in year one, and anybody who says otherwise has never weighed a harvest. Grow calories, not salad: potatoes, maize, beans, squash, sweet potato.
• Rough scale: a well-run intensive bed yields around 3 kg of potatoes per square metre, roughly 2,300 kcal. Feeding one adult for a year is therefore hundreds of square metres of beds even before losses, storms and pests. Plan for a meaningful supplement, not self-sufficiency.
• Animals: hens are the best return — four to six birds give around twenty eggs a week on scraps and forage, and need almost no infrastructure. Rabbits breed fast on greens. A goat needs grazing and a year of learning. Anything larger needs winter feed you probably can't grow.
• Fishing, trapping and foraging fill gaps but rarely carry a household. Trade labour for food long before you go hungry.
§ Work the whole year at once
• Sow, harvest, preserve, store, and hold seed back — every year, in that order. The failure mode is eating the seed corn in a bad autumn.
• Store for the hungry gap: late winter to first harvest is when the unprepared starve in the second year, not the first.
• Wood cut and split this winter burns next winter. Fuel is always a year ahead; wood at 20% moisture gives you the heat, wet wood gives you creosote and a chimney fire.
§ Make the temporary permanent
• Water: a well, a spring, or roof catchment into proper covered storage with a treatment step. Fix it once instead of carrying buckets for a decade.
• Sanitation: a pit that can be moved, or proper composting. Human waste needs a full year at composting temperatures before it goes anywhere near food crops; until you are confident, put it on fuel wood and fruit trees, never on salad.
• Shelter: a stove that burns efficiently, insulation, a dry store, a workshop bench.
§ Skills, spares and consumables
• Somebody must learn to sew, sharpen, solder, splice rope, repair a bicycle, splint a limb, deliver a baby, keep bees, save seed, butcher an animal. Teach each other; a skill spread across four people survives one funeral.
• The consumables that quietly end things: needles and thread, files and blades, fixings, lamp wicks, boot repair, glasses (keep a spare pair and your written prescription), sanitary supplies, contraception. Pregnancy without medical care is a serious risk and a decision worth making deliberately.
§ Governance and records
• However decisions are being made, make it explicit and reviewable. Written rules, a way to change them, and a common store kept separate from private property with a record. Vagueness is what splits groups.
• Agree in advance how you treat people who arrive. Absolutism in either direction ends badly.
• Keep a real journal: weather, planting dates, what stored well, what failed, births, deaths, trades. That record is the only reason year two is better than year one.
• Keep a box of documents, deeds, ID and qualifications, dry and findable. Normal life may come back, and you will want to prove who you are.

guides.title: Go or stay
guides.summary: Staying is the default. What has to be true before you leave, and how to decide it in advance rather than at 3 a.m.
guides.text:
Home is your stores, your shelter, your water and the people who know you. The road is where you have none of that and are a stranger. Most people who leave without a destination arrive somewhere worse. Staying is the default, and the burden of proof is on going.
§ Leave only if one of these is true
• The building is unsurvivable: fire, flood, structural damage, no heat in deep cold, or contamination you cannot shut out.
• Water and sanitation cannot be solved where you are, and won't be.
• Somebody needs medical care that exists elsewhere and can still be reached.
• Violence in the immediate area is beyond your ability to avoid.
Being frightened, bored or short of a few days' food is not on that list.
§ Going requires three things, not one
• A destination that expects you. Not "north", not "my cousin's, probably". A named place, and if possible people there who know you're coming.
• A route you can actually complete with the fuel in the tank or the legs you have. Fuel is roughly half of what it says once traffic sets in; on foot, plan 4–5 km/h on road, 3 km/h off it, and add an hour for every 600 m of climb.
• The means to arrive with something. Water, food for three days, medication, documents, cash, warm dry layers, a torch.
Missing any one of the three and you are not evacuating, you are becoming a refugee.
§ Timing decides more than the decision
• Roads jam within hours of a mass decision. The workable windows are usually the first 6–12 hours, or several days later once the surge has cleared.
• Decide the trigger in advance and write it as an if-then: "if water hasn't returned by day X", "if the fire reaches the ridge", "if indoor temperature is below 10 °C and the fuel is gone". Pre-commitment prevents both dithering and panic.
• Know your choke points — bridges, tunnels, a single pass — and hold two alternative routes on paper. Assume signage, traffic control and fuel stations are absent.
§ Sheltering in place has hard limits too
• No water at all is a three-day clock. Solve that or the decision makes itself.
• Sealing a building against an airborne plume works for hours to days, not weeks. It buys you time to move, not a permanent answer.
• If you stay, harden it: water, sanitation, heat, food, neighbours. Then set a review date instead of reopening the question every night.
§ The middle options
• Send some, keep some: the vulnerable to a relative or a shelter, one or two capable adults holding the house.
• Official shelters are not a failure. They have water, sanitation, heat and medical staff. They are also crowded and loud, and most won't take pets — bring ID, medication and your own bedding.
• Leaving is reversible if you leave the house sound. Lock up, turn off gas and water at the mains if you're going for good, leave a note where your household agreed, photograph the contents.
§ If you go
Travel in daylight, tell someone your route and expected arrival, keep the group together, and stop before you're exhausted. Anyone can walk 20 km once; almost nobody can do it three days running with a pack and no plan for water.

guides.title: Coming home
guides.summary: Re-entry hurts people because the danger looks over. How to check a building, restore utilities safely, and come back into normal life.
guides.text:
People get injured coming home. The emergency looks finished, so caution goes, and the hazards left behind — gas, live wires, contaminated water, an unstable wall, a flooded floor and an electric drill — do the damage the disaster didn't.
§ Before you go in
• If any authority is still saying "not yet", wait. Approach in daylight, never alone, and tell somebody where you are.
• Walk the outside first: leaning or bulging walls, new cracks, a sagging roofline, a shifted foundation, a leaning chimney. If it looks wrong, it is wrong — don't go in.
• Treat every downed cable as live and stay 10 m (30 ft) away, including anything it is touching, fence or puddle.
• If you smell gas or hear hissing, don't switch anything on or off, don't use a phone inside, leave, shut the supply off at the meter only if you can do it from outside, and report it.
§ Restoring utilities
• Switch everything off at the consumer unit before restoring power, then bring circuits back one at a time and watch for smells and heat.
• Never touch electrical equipment while standing in water, and never restore power to a circuit that has been submerged until it has been checked.
• Before opening the stop tap, look for burst pipes; a system that froze will empty into the ceiling within minutes.
• Ventilate for an hour before you spend time inside. Torch, not a naked flame.
• Boots, gloves, long sleeves and a mask. Flood residue is sewage, mould and whatever was in the shed upstream.
§ What has to go, and what doesn't
• Anything porous that got flood water and can't be washed hot: carpet, underlay, mattresses, upholstery, insulation, and plasterboard to 30–50 cm above the tide line.
• Mould establishes in 24–48 hours. Open everything, get air moving, dry aggressively, then disinfect hard surfaces with a 1:10 household bleach solution where sewage is involved.
• Throw out food that touched flood water, including screw-top jars and crimped bottle caps — neither is watertight. Tins can be saved: remove the label, wash, disinfect, relabel with a marker.
• Judge the freezer by temperature and ice crystals, not smell. Still holding ice crystals means refreezable; above 4 °C for more than a couple of hours means gone.
• Photograph everything before you clear it, keep receipts, and don't throw away the proof of what you lost.
§ The other re-entry
Coming back into a working society is its own adjustment, and the flat, angry, exhausted phase usually arrives after the crisis rather than during it.
• Expect bureaucracy: ID, banking, claims, forms that assume nothing unusual happened. Start the paperwork early and keep copies.
• Expect to be out of step with people who weren't there. They will want the short version. You may not want to give it.
• Sleep, daylight, food and routine are still the medicine. So is telling somebody the whole thing once, properly.
• Watch children for weeks, not days. They process late, and they take their reading of events from the adults.
§ Before you relax
Debrief the household while it's fresh: what worked, what nearly cost you, what you'd never be without again. Rebuild the water, food, fuel and medical stores now, at normal prices, in a quiet week. Then go and knock on the doors of the people who helped you.

guides.title: Water at household scale
guides.summary: How much you actually need, where a house hides it, and how to make doubtful water safe with what you have.
guides.text:
Finding a stream is the easy part. Running a household on water you carry and treat, every day, without anybody getting ill, is the real problem.
§ How much
• 3 litres per person per day for drinking in a temperate climate. Double it in heat or with hard physical work.
• 15 litres per person per day covers drinking, cooking and basic hygiene — the humanitarian minimum. Below about 7.5 litres, hygiene starts to fail and people get sick.
• 4 litres (1 gallon) per person per day is the standard planning figure for stored supplies. Two weeks stored is 56 litres for one person, 224 for a family of four — a stack of containers, not a shelf.
• Don't ration drinking water. Ration washing, laundry and flushing instead, and go and find more. Dark urine means drink more; you cannot train yourself to need less.
§ Water already in the house
• Hot water cylinder: 150–190 litres (40–50 gallons) of drinkable water. Kill the power or gas to it first, close the cold inlet, open a hot tap upstairs to let air in, then draw from the drain valve at the bottom. The first litre carries sediment.
• Toilet cistern (the tank, not the bowl) unless it holds a chemical block. The bowl is for flushing only.
• Pipework: open the highest tap in the house to let air in, then drain from the lowest.
• Ice, tinned vegetable liquid, the bath you filled in the first hour.
• A rain butt, a swimming pool or a hot tub is washing and flushing water. Treat pool water as chemically loaded, not merely dirty.
§ Making it safe
• Boiling is the only method that deals with everything. A rolling boil for 1 minute; 3 minutes above about 2,000 m (6,500 ft), where water boils cooler. It costs fuel, so boil what you'll drink, not what you'll wash in.
• Unscented household bleach at 5–6% sodium hypochlorite: 2 drops per litre (8 drops per gallon) for clear water, double for cold or cloudy, wait 30 minutes. It should smell faintly of chlorine afterwards; if not, redose and wait another 15 minutes. Bleach loses strength — it is roughly half-dead after a year on the shelf.
• Filters rated 0.2 micron or finer remove bacteria and protozoa but not viruses. Chlorine and iodine do not reliably kill Cryptosporidium. A filter followed by chlorine covers both; boiling covers both on its own.
• Cloudy water first: let it settle, then pour through folded cloth or a sand-and-charcoal column. Chemicals and UV are wasted on turbid water.
• SODIS: clear PET bottles no larger than 2 litres, laid on their side in full sun for 6 hours (two days if overcast). Only for clear water, and it does not work through glass or in shade.
§ What treatment cannot fix
Boiling concentrates chemical contamination rather than removing it. If water may carry fuel, solvent, pesticide, industrial run-off or heavy metals, do not boil it and do not drink it — find another source. Salt water needs distillation; you cannot filter or boil salt out of it.
§ Storing and carrying
• Food-grade containers, dated, kept cool and dark. Treated water keeps about six months, and anything you draw again is worth a fresh chlorine dose.
• Never reuse a container that held anything but food or drink. One badly rinsed chemical jug poisons the batch.
• 20 litres weighs 20 kg. Carry two 10-litre containers rather than one big one, and use a cart for anything more.
• Label drinking containers and washing containers, keep them apart, and never put untreated water in a drinking one.
• Roof catchment: discard the first flush after a dry spell, screen the inlet, keep the tank covered and dark, and treat before drinking. Avoid run-off from asbestos, lead flashing or treated shingles.

guides.title: Sanitation and human waste
guides.summary: The thing that actually kills people after a disaster. Where waste goes, how hands get clean, and what to do when someone has diarrhoea.
guides.text:
In every large emergency the killer on the record is the same: diarrhoeal disease, spread from faeces to mouths by way of hands, flies, food and water. It takes small children and old people first, and it is almost entirely preventable with buckets, soap and discipline. Give it the same weight as water and food.
§ The rule
Human waste never touches hands, food, water or flies. Every arrangement below is just a way of enforcing that.
§ Where it goes
• Sewer still working, water available: keep flushing. A normal toilet takes about 6–9 litres of grey water poured in fast. Stop instantly if drains gurgle, back up or smell — you are downstream of something that has failed, and a backed-up sewer inside the house is a disaster of its own.
• Bucket system, indoors: two lined buckets with lids. Urine in one, faeces and paper in the other, covered after each use with a scoop of sawdust, dry soil, leaves, shredded paper or wood ash. The cover material is what stops the smell and the flies; keep more of it than you think you need.
• Pit or trench latrine, outdoors: at least 30 m (100 ft) from any well, spring, stream or water store, and downhill of it, with the pit floor at least 1.5–2 m above the water table. Dig it deep and narrow — 30 cm wide, a metre or more deep — with a solid cover, a slab either side to stand on, and a mound and channel so rain runs away rather than in. Allow roughly 60–90 litres of pit volume per person per year, and site the replacement before the first is full.
• One person, moving: a cat hole 15–20 cm (6–8 in) deep, at least 60 m (200 ft) from water, camp and trail, and filled in.
• Urine is nearly sterile as it leaves the body and is mostly a volume problem: 1–2 litres per person per day. Keep it out of the solids — separating the two roughly halves the smell and the fly problem. Diluted about 1:10 with water it is a good nitrogen feed for fruit trees and non-leaf crops; don't put it on anything you eat raw.
§ Handwashing is the intervention
Handwashing with soap cuts diarrhoeal disease by around a third — no other single thing you do comes close.
• Put a washing point immediately outside the toilet and a second where food is prepared. A tippy-tap — a hung jerrycan tipped by a foot rope, soap on a string — uses a fraction of a litre per wash and nobody touches a tap.
• Wash after the toilet, after nappies or a sick person, after waste or animals, before preparing food, before eating.
• Twenty seconds with soap, under the nails included. Soap matters far more than the volume of water. Alcohol gel of 60% or more is a backup only — it fails on visibly dirty hands and does nothing against norovirus or Cryptosporidium.
§ When somebody has diarrhoea
• Rehydrate immediately: 1 litre of clean water, 6 level teaspoons of sugar, half a level teaspoon of salt. Small sips, continuously. An adult losing fluid fast may need 3 litres or more a day; keep giving it even if they vomit. Never make it saltier than the recipe.
• Get help if there is blood in the stool, a stiff or sunken look with no urine for 8 hours or more, confusion, or a small child who will not drink.
• Isolate: their own bucket, towel and cup. One person cares for them, and that person washes.
• Disinfect with household bleach: 1:10 for vomit, faeces and the toilet itself; 1:100 for floors, handles and general surfaces. Leave it wet on the surface for at least a minute. Mix fresh daily — diluted bleach loses strength within about 24 hours.
• Boil, don't just chlorinate, drinking water for the household until it has passed.
§ The rest of the chain
• Flies breed in exposed waste and land on food. Lids and covers on everything, and food kept under cloth or mesh.
• Nappies and children's faeces are the highest-risk material in any household. Bag them, cover them, wash like it matters.
• Greywater to a rubble-filled soakaway well away from the kitchen and any drinking source. Never let it stand.
• Rubbish and food scraps buried or burned away from the house; they bring rats.
• Menstrual supplies: stock more than you think, plus soap, a covered bucket for washables and somewhere sunny to dry them.
• Burying the dead: at least 30 m from any water source, 1.5 m above the water table, and marked. The infection risk from bodies is usually overstated, but it is real for cholera and haemorrhagic illness — gloves, and wash afterwards.

guides.title: Food storage and preservation
guides.summary: Eat the fridge first, store the rest properly, and never guess at canning — botulism gives no warning.
guides.text:
Two jobs: get through what's already in the house before it spoils, and put the rest somewhere it will still be food in a year.
§ The order you eat things
• Fridge first, 4 hours. An unopened fridge holds safe temperature about four hours. Cook or eat what's in it today.
• Freezer next. A full freezer holds roughly 48 hours, a half-full one about 24. Pack the gaps with bottles of water — a full freezer stays cold far longer, and the ice is drinking water later.
• Then dry stores. Rice, pasta, pulses, tins, oil, salt, sugar.
• The danger zone is 5–60 °C (40–140 °F). Perishable food more than 2 hours above 4 °C is suspect, 1 hour if it's above 32 °C (90 °F). Judge by a thermometer, not by smell — most of what makes you ill has no taste and no odour. When in doubt, throw it out; a day's food is cheaper than a week of diarrhoea.
§ Dry storage
• Cool, dark, dry, sealed against pests. Shelf life roughly halves for every 10 °C rise, so a cupboard at 15 °C keeps food perhaps twice as long as one at 25 °C.
• In food-grade buckets with mylar liners and oxygen absorbers, white rice, wheat, rolled oats, pasta, dried maize and dried beans keep 10–30 years. Salt and sugar keep indefinitely (sugar needs no oxygen absorber — it sets like concrete).
• What doesn't keep: brown rice, wholemeal flour, nuts, seeds and cooking oil all go rancid in about six months at room temperature, because of the oil in them. Buy small and rotate hard.
• Freeze new grain and flour for 72 hours at −18 °C to kill weevil eggs before it goes into storage.
• Mice chew through plastic. Use metal bins, or buckets somewhere they can't reach.
• Date everything. First in, first out, and a written list of what is where.
§ Root cellar and cool store
• Roots (carrot, beet, turnip) want 0–4 °C and 90–95% humidity — damp sand or sawdust in boxes.
• Potatoes: 4–7 °C, dark and ventilated. Colder and the starch turns sweet; light turns them green and toxic.
• Onions, garlic and squash want cool and dry, not humid.
• Keep apples away from potatoes and roots — the ethylene they give off makes everything else sprout.
§ Preserving
• Drying is the cheapest. Fruit to leathery with no beads of moisture when squeezed, vegetables to brittle. Meat for jerky must reach 71 °C (160 °F) before drying, or you preserve the bacteria along with the meat.
• Fermenting needs only salt: a 2–3% brine by weight, everything held under the liquid, 18–22 °C. Sauerkraut and salt pickles keep for months and add vitamin C.
• Salting and smoking: cold-smoking preserves but needs a tested recipe and curing salts; hot-smoking is cooking, and buys days rather than months. Don't improvise a cure.
• Canning is where people die, so be precise:
• High-acid foods (pH 4.6 or below — most fruit, jams, properly acidified tomatoes, vinegar pickles) can be processed in a boiling water bath.
• Low-acid foods (vegetables, beans, maize, meat, fish, soups) must be pressure canned at 116–121 °C (240–250 °F). A boiling water bath cannot reach the temperature that kills Clostridium botulinum spores. There is no workaround. No oven canning, no dishwasher, no "my grandmother always did it".
• Follow a tested recipe including its altitude adjustment — both boiling times and pressures increase with elevation.
• Lids are consumable. Stock them.
• Botulinum toxin does not smell, taste or discolour food. Discard any jar with a bulging lid, a broken seal, spurting liquid, mould or an off smell without tasting it. Boiling home-canned low-acid food for 10 minutes (plus a minute per 300 m / 1,000 ft of altitude) destroys the toxin, and is worth doing as a matter of routine.

guides.title: Cooking and heat without power
guides.summary: Carbon monoxide is the thing that kills after the power cut. Then: burning less fuel, and heating one room instead of a house.
guides.text:
More people die of carbon monoxide and house fires after a power cut than of cold. Read the first section before you light anything.
§ Carbon monoxide, first and last
• Never burn charcoal indoors. Not in a fireplace, not in a garage, not in a tent, not in an open doorway. A barbecue in a room kills a family overnight, and it is the single most common way people die in a blackout.
• Never run a generator indoors, in a garage, in a basement or within 6 m (20 ft) of a window, door or vent — including the neighbour's.
• Camping stoves are for outdoors or a genuinely ventilated space, and for cooking only, never heating.
• Unvented paraffin or catalytic heaters need a window open and an oxygen depletion sensor. They also dump a lot of water vapour into the room; expect condensation and mould.
• CO has no smell. Get a battery carbon monoxide alarm and put it where people sleep. Symptoms are headache, nausea, dizziness and confusion in more than one person at once, better when outdoors — if that happens, get everyone out into fresh air immediately and don't go back in.
§ Burn less fuel
• Lid on the pot. A lid alone can halve the fuel to boil.
• A windshield outdoors saves more than any stove upgrade.
• Simmer, don't boil hard. A rolling boil is not hotter, just faster to empty.
• Retained-heat cooking: bring beans, grain or stew to the boil for 10–15 minutes, then seal the pot in a well-insulated box — a haybox, a duvet, a sleeping bag in a crate — for 2–4 hours. It saves 50–80% of the fuel and can't burn the food.
• A pressure cooker turns a two-hour pot of beans into 30 minutes and pays for its weight in fuel within a week.
• Soak dried beans and grains overnight; it cuts cooking time by a third or more.
• Cook once a day for the whole household. One fire, one pot, less smoke and less smell for anyone to notice.
• Solar cookers work in clear sun, reaching 90–150 °C. Slow, silent, free, and useless under cloud.
§ Heating
• Heat the person, then the room, then never the house. Layers, hats indoors, insulation under you as well as over you — the floor and the mattress steal more heat than the air.
• Choose one room, preferably small, south-facing and away from the wind. Close doors, hang blankets over doorways and windows at night, block draughts at the bottom of doors, and put everyone in it.
• Sleep together and sleep off the floor. Two people under shared blankets need far less fuel than two people in separate rooms.
• A "flowerpot candle heater" is a myth. One candle is about 80 watts; it will not heat a room, but it will burn the house down if you leave it.
§ Wood
• Burn seasoned wood at 20% moisture or less. Wet wood gives half the heat and coats the flue in creosote, which is how houses burn down in month two. Sweep the flue.
• Never burn treated, painted or pressure-treated timber, chipboard or driftwood. The fumes are genuinely poisonous and the salt in driftwood destroys the stove.
• Plan roughly 3–5 cords (11–18 m³) for a full northern winter of whole-house heating, or 1–2 cords to keep one room going. Cut it a year ahead — this winter's wood should already be dry.
• Keep a fire extinguisher and a lid to smother a pan fire. Never put water on burning fat or oil; the lid or a damp cloth, and turn the heat off.

guides.title: Growing food and seed saving
guides.summary: Grow calories, not salad. Realistic yields, what to plant first, and how to keep seed that comes true next year.
guides.text:
A garden started after the lorries stop will not feed you this year. Started now, it feeds you next year and every year after. Both facts matter; plan around the second and be honest about the first.
§ Grow calories
• The crops that carry a household are potatoes, maize, dried beans, winter squash and sweet potato. Salad leaves are almost pure water — pleasant, not food.
• Rough numbers: a well-run intensive bed gives about 3 kg of potatoes per square metre, roughly 2,300 kcal. An adult needs about 2,000 kcal a day. Do the arithmetic and you find that hundreds of square metres feed one person for a year, before you allow for pests, drought and a bad autumn.
• So aim to supplement heavily in year one and build towards more. A 100 m² plot planted in staples is a serious contribution; it is not independence.
• Plant the fast things first if you're starting late: radish 25 days, salad leaves 30, bush beans 55, courgette 50, then maize and potatoes at 90–120.
• Perennials pay back for a decade and take years to start: fruit trees 3–5 years, asparagus 3, rhubarb and berries 2. Plant them the first spring, whatever else is happening.
§ Soil and inputs
• Compost everything: kitchen scraps, weeds, leaves, cardboard, ash in small amounts. A hot heap needs volume — roughly a cubic metre — and turning.
• Urine diluted about 1:10 is a good free nitrogen feed. Use it on soil around fruit, maize and roots; not on leaves you eat raw, and not neat.
• Wood ash supplies potassium and raises pH. A dusting, not a dump — it will make soil too alkaline fast.
• Human waste needs a full year of hot composting before it goes near food crops. Until then, fruit trees and fuel wood only.
• Mulch holds water and suppresses weeds, and water is usually the constraint you didn't plan for.
§ Saving seed
• Only open-pollinated or heirloom varieties come true. Seed saved from an F1 hybrid gives you a lottery ticket, not the plant you liked. Check your packets now and buy open-pollinated where it matters.
• Easy savers — self-pollinating, save from any healthy plant: beans, peas, lettuce, tomatoes. Start here.
• Harder — they cross with anything nearby: squash and cucumber (hand-pollinate and tape the flowers shut), brassicas and carrots and beets (biennial, they seed in their second year), maize (needs 100+ plants to avoid inbreeding and roughly 200 m of isolation from another variety).
• Save from your best plants, and always from several — one plant's seed is a genetic dead end.
• Wet-seeded fruit (tomato, cucumber): scoop seed and pulp into a jar of water, ferment 2–3 days until it scums over, then rinse until clean and dry on a plate, not paper.
• Dry to the point of brittleness. A bean should shatter rather than dent when struck. Damp seed rots or germinates in the packet.
• Store cool, dark and dry in paper or glass. The rule of thumb: temperature in °F plus relative humidity in % should be under 100.
• Realistic viability if stored well: onion and parsnip 1 year; maize, pepper and carrot 2–3; beans and peas 3; tomato, brassica, cucumber and squash 4–5; lettuce 5 or more. Test a batch on damp kitchen paper before you commit a bed to it.
• Label everything at the moment you pick it. You will not remember, and unlabelled seed is a wasted season.

guides.title: Medical beyond first aid
guides.summary: Chronic medication, infection, and being honest about what needs a clinician when there isn't one.
guides.text:
First aid handles the first ten minutes. This is about the weeks after: the medicines somebody takes every day, wounds that turn, illness that doesn't pass, and knowing which problems you genuinely cannot solve at home.
§ Prevention is nearly all of it
Clean water, handwashing with soap, safe food, working sanitation and enough sleep prevent more illness than any kit you can buy. Beyond that: keep vaccinations current, get a tetanus booster if yours is over ten years old, and get the medical and dental work you've been putting off done while services exist.
§ Chronic medication is the first crisis
• Write a list, now, for every person: drug, dose, what it's for, prescriber. Photograph the labels. That list is worth more than anything in a first aid kit.
• Count days of supply. Ask your pharmacist or doctor about a longer supply for emergencies; many will agree if you explain why.
• Some drugs are dangerous to stop abruptly — beta blockers, steroids, anti-epileptics, benzodiazepines, opioids, some antidepressants. Rebound, seizures and adrenal crisis are real risks. Find out which of yours are in that group while you can still ask.
• Insulin: unopened vials keep at 2–8 °C; in use, most keep about 28 days at room temperature. Heat above 30 °C degrades it. A cellar, an evaporative cooler or an insulated box with cool water buys weeks.
• Oxygen, dialysis and CPAP make somebody dependent on power or on a delivery. That is a plan you make on the first day, not in the second week.
• No dosing tables here for prescription drugs. Keep the label and the patient leaflet, don't improvise doses, and don't share medicines between people.
§ Infection
Recognise it early, because untreated infection is the classic quiet killer.
• Local signs: increasing pain after day two, spreading redness, heat, swelling, pus, red streaks running from the wound, a wound that reopens.
• Systemic signs: fever, shivering, fast breathing, fast heart rate, confusion, feeling far worse than the injury explains. That combination is sepsis. It needs a hospital, and there is no home treatment for it.
• Wounds: irrigate hard with plenty of clean water — 250–500 ml squeezed from a bottle is not too much — and get the grit out. Don't close a dirty wound, a puncture, a bite or anything more than a few hours old: pack it, dress it, let it heal from the bottom, and look at it every day when you change the dressing.
• Antibiotics: partial courses breed resistance, most sore throats and coughs are viral, and treating blind usually treats the wrong thing. If you'll be genuinely remote, ask a clinician about a standby course and the conditions for using it. That is a medical conversation, not a stockpiling exercise.
§ Things you should know cold
• Burns: cool under running water for 20 minutes, within three hours of the injury. No ice, no butter. Cover with cling film laid on, not wrapped. Anything bigger than the patient's palm, or on face, hands, feet or genitals, or right around a limb, or white and leathery, needs a hospital.
• Dehydration kills more people than the illness that caused it. Oral rehydration solution: 1 litre clean water, 6 level teaspoons sugar, half a level teaspoon salt, sipped continuously.
• Fractures: splint including the joint above and below, elevate, and check fingers or toes for warmth, colour and feeling before and after. An open fracture, a deformed limb, or a limb that goes cold or numb needs a surgeon.
• Chest pain, stroke signs, a rigid painful abdomen, a head injury with worsening drowsiness, difficulty breathing: all need a hospital. If there isn't one, keep them warm, still and hydrated if awake, write down times and observations, and say plainly what you can and cannot do.
• Childbirth almost always proceeds by itself. Keep the baby warm, dry and skin-to-skin, don't pull, and watch the mother for heavy bleeding.
Finally: do a real first aid or first responder course. Two days in a room with an instructor is worth more than every guide you will ever read, including this one.

guides.title: Dental
guides.summary: Teeth do not heal on their own. Prevention, temporary repairs, and the swelling that is a genuine emergency.
guides.text:
Toothache is one of the most common serious problems in any long emergency, and dentistry is the one field where doing nothing reliably makes things worse. A tooth that hurts today is an abscess in a fortnight. Get outstanding dental work done now, while there are dentists.
§ Prevention is the whole game
• Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and clean between the teeth. Two minutes, properly, beats anything you can do later.
• Stock spare brushes, paste and floss — they are light, cheap and last for years. A brush should be replaced every three months or so.
• If paste runs out: brushing with plain water still removes plaque. Bicarbonate of soda works as a dentifrice. A salt rinse — half a teaspoon in 250 ml of warm water — soothes gums but does not clean teeth.
• Sugar is the driver. In an emergency diet heavy on sweetened drinks, jam and boiled sweets, expect decay to accelerate sharply, especially in children.
§ Temporary repairs
• Lost filling or broken tooth: clean the cavity, dry it, and pack it with over-the-counter temporary filling material (zinc oxide and eugenol), then bite gently to seat it. Sugar-free gum is a stopgap for an hour, not a week. A packet of temporary filling material costs almost nothing and belongs in the kit.
• Knocked-out adult tooth: hold it by the crown, never the root. Rinse briefly in milk or saline if dirty — don't scrub it and don't let it dry. Put it straight back in the socket and have the person bite on a clean cloth. If that isn't possible, keep it in milk or the person's own saliva, never water, and reach a dentist within 30–60 minutes. Baby teeth are never put back.
• Broken orthodontic wire: bend it flat, or cover the end with orthodontic wax or sugar-free gum. Denture sore: stop wearing it and rinse with salt water until the ulcer heals.
§ Toothache
• Over-the-counter painkillers taken to the label. For most adults who can take both, paracetamol (acetaminophen) and ibuprofen alternated control dental pain better than either alone.
• Clove oil (eugenol) on a scrap of cotton wool held against the tooth gives real relief. Keep it off the gum and tongue, where it burns.
• Cold compress on the outside of the cheek. Never heat over a swollen face — warmth spreads infection.
• Sleep propped up; lying flat increases the throbbing. Keep temperature extremes and sugar off that side.
§ The emergency
A dental abscess can become life-threatening when it spreads into the floor of the mouth or the neck. Treat these as an emergency needing a clinician and antibiotics, immediately:
• Swelling spreading to the eye, the jawline or the neck.
• Fever with facial swelling.
• Difficulty swallowing, opening the mouth, or breathing, or a raised tongue.
If there is genuinely no help available, warm salt-water rinses several times an hour can encourage a pointing abscess to drain into the mouth, which relieves pressure. Keep fluids going, keep the person upright, and keep watching the airway. Be clear-eyed: this is a holding action, not a treatment.
§ Don't attempt an extraction
Without training, instruments and anaesthetic, the usual results are a fractured root left in the jaw, bleeding you can't stop, and a worse infection than the one you started with. It is almost always better to manage pain and infection and wait for someone who can do it properly.
If a tooth is already lost or a socket is bleeding: bite firmly on rolled gauze for 20–30 minutes, don't rinse, spit or use a straw for 24 hours, and expect a spike of severe pain around day three to five if the clot is lost — salt rinses and painkillers, and keep it clean.

guides.title: Power and fuel
guides.summary: Work out what genuinely needs electricity, size it in watt-hours, and store fuel without burning the house down.
guides.text:
Most of what you'd like to power, you don't need. Start by separating the loads that keep somebody alive from the ones that keep you comfortable, and size for the first list.
§ What actually needs power
• Life-critical: oxygen concentrator, CPAP, a fridge holding insulin, a powered wheelchair, a well pump.
• High value, tiny draw: LED lighting, a radio, torches, charging phones and power banks.
• Comfort: everything else. Heating and cooking by electricity is off the table on any small system — resistive heat eats a battery bank in an hour.
§ Do the arithmetic in watt-hours
• Phone charge: about 15 Wh. LED lamp: 5 W, so 50 Wh for a ten-hour night across a few lamps. Laptop: 50 W. CPAP: 30–60 W, so 300–500 Wh a night. A domestic fridge: 1–2 kWh a day, which is a serious system on its own.
• A 100 W solar panel makes roughly 300–500 Wh on a clear summer day. In midwinter at a northern latitude under cloud, assume a quarter of that.
• A 12 V 100 Ah lead-acid battery holds 1.2 kWh nominal, but only about half is usable without wrecking it — call it 600 Wh. LiFePO4 of the same rating gives you most of its capacity and thousands of cycles rather than hundreds.
• Running loads directly at 12 V avoids the 10–15% an inverter wastes, so USB and 12 V lighting are worth building around.
§ Generators
• Size it to charge batteries and run the fridge for a couple of hours, then switch it off. Running a generator continuously to power a lamp burns a tank a day.
• Fuel burn is roughly 0.5–1 litre an hour for a 2 kW inverter set at half load.
• Outdoors only — never in a garage, porch, basement or within 6 m (20 ft) of any window, door or vent, yours or a neighbour's. Carbon monoxide from generators kills people every storm season.
• Never backfeed through a wall socket. It can electrocute line workers and start a fire. A transfer switch or interlock fitted by an electrician is the only safe way to feed a house.
• A generator is audible for a kilometre and tells everybody who has power. Run it in daylight, when other noise exists, and only when it's earning its fuel.
§ Storing fuel
• Petrol goes stale in 3–6 months, up to about a year with stabiliser. Diesel keeps 6–12 months and longer with a biocide — watch for water and microbial growth in the tank. Propane and butane keep indefinitely and are the easiest fuels to store safely.
• Approved containers only, clearly labelled, out of the living space, in the shade, away from any pilot light or ignition source. Check your local limits on domestic quantities; 25–30 litres is a common cap.
• Petrol vapour is heavier than air and explosive. Never store it in a basement, under stairs, or anywhere vapour can pool and find a flame.
• Rotate: put stored fuel into the car and refill the can, on a date you write down.
§ Batteries and small power
• Keep lead-acid batteries charged; left flat they sulphate dead within weeks. Store lithium cells at around half charge, out of the cold.
• Rechargeable AA cells and a small solar charger run headlamps and a radio essentially forever, at a fraction of the cost of alkalines.
• Charge every power bank in the first hour of an outage, and keep one untouched as a reserve for communications.
• A car with an inverter is a generator you already own — 150–300 W from the accessory socket, more from a fused connection at the battery. The battery alone flattens in an hour or two and then the car won't start, so run the engine to charge, outdoors.
• Fuse everything, use the right cable size, and keep a torch where you can find it in the dark.

guides.title: Vehicles and mobility
guides.summary: Fuel and traffic are the limits, not the vehicle. Keeping a car useful, and the bicycle and boots that outlast it.
guides.text:
A car is a fast way to travel for as long as there is fuel and the road is clear, and neither lasts. Plan for the car, then plan for its absence.
§ Habits that pay once
• Keep the tank above half. It is the single cheapest preparation anybody can make. No power means no pumps: filling stations stop within hours of a grid failure.
• Keep the vehicle serviceable: tyres including the spare and the pressure in it, oil, coolant, belts, wipers, and a battery that isn't more than four or five years old.
• Keep paper maps in the car. Every satnav is one dead phone away from useless, and this app is the other half of that answer.
§ What lives in the car
Water, warm and dry layers, sturdy boots, a torch with spare cells, a jump pack or leads, a tow strap, basic tools, a tyre plug kit and a 12 V compressor, a first aid kit, spare fuses, duct tape, a hi-vis vest, a folding shovel, traction boards or a bag of grit, cash in small notes, and a phone cable that fits everything.
§ Range and driving
• Economy falls apart in stop-start traffic. Steady 80 km/h (50 mph) instead of 110 (70) is worth roughly 20–25% more distance from the same tank.
• Idling burns fuel for nothing. In a queue, switch off.
• Weight and roof loads cost fuel. Take what you need and no more.
• Siphoning modern cars mostly doesn't work — filler necks have anti-siphon valves and screens. Never siphon by mouth: a mouthful of petrol in the lungs causes chemical pneumonitis and can kill.
• Don't drive into floodwater. Thirty centimetres (1 ft) of moving water will float a car; 15 cm will take an adult off their feet. You cannot see whether the road is still there.
• In snow, a car is a survivable shelter — but only if you clear the exhaust pipe before running the engine for heat, and run it in short bursts with a window cracked. A blocked exhaust fills the cabin with carbon monoxide.
§ Leaving in a vehicle
• Know two or three routes out and where the choke points are: bridges, tunnels, a single mountain pass, a motorway junction. Those are where a mass movement stops.
• Leave early or leave late. The middle is a queue with no fuel in it.
• Travel in daylight, keep the group in one vehicle if you can, and tell somebody at the far end that you're coming.
§ When the fuel is gone
• The bicycle is the answer most people overlook. 25–60 km a day is unremarkable, it needs no fuel, it carries 20–40 kg with panniers and far more with a trailer, and it's quiet. Keep tubes, patches, a pump, a spare chain, brake pads and cables, and learn to fix a puncture properly before you need to.
• On foot: 4–5 km/h on a road, about 3 km/h off it, plus an hour for every 600 m of ascent. Most people carry 20 kg without ruining themselves; well-fitted boots and blister care decide your range more than fitness does.
• A handcart, a wheelbarrow or a child's trailer moves water and firewood daily, and in a world without fuel that is more useful than a car in the drive.
• Look after feet the way you would look after an engine. Dry socks, trimmed nails, blisters covered before they burst, boots broken in long before the day you need them.

guides.title: Communications discipline
guides.summary: Listen far more than you transmit. Realistic ranges, a household plan that works on paper, and what never goes over the air.
guides.text:
Communications is two problems that pull against each other: getting information, and not broadcasting your own. Solve the first by listening, and the second by transmitting rarely, briefly and without content worth having.
§ Receive first
• A battery or wind-up radio with AM, FM and shortwave gives you national and international news while emitting nothing at all. Buy one, and keep spare cells with it.
• In the US, an NOAA weather radio (162.400–162.550 MHz) carries hazard alerts directly from the National Weather Service.
• A scanner or a cheap software-defined radio lets you hear local services and other users, which tells you more about your area than any broadcast will.
• Write down what you hear with the time and the source. Two fixed listening windows a day beats a radio muttering in the corner all day, which only produces anxiety.
§ Transmitting is a signal about you
Anything you transmit tells anyone listening that you exist, roughly where you are, and — from what you say — what you have. Direction-finding a repeated transmission is not exotic; it is a hobbyist's afternoon. Assume every transmission is heard by someone you'd rather not meet.
• Keep transmissions short and scheduled. A five-minute window at 08:00 and 18:00 is a plan; a radio left keyed up all day is an advertisement.
• Never state over the air: your address, how much food, fuel, medicine or ammunition you have, who is alone, when the house is empty, or that anyone is ill or injured in a way that makes you look weak.
• Agree simple phrases in advance — "we're fine", "come now", "do not come", "meet at the second place". Not code words that sound like a film; ordinary words with agreed meanings.
• Encryption on the amateur bands is generally illegal, and obvious ciphers attract attention. Brevity and vagueness serve better.
§ What actually works, and how far
• FRS / PMR446 handhelds: licence-free, low power, and realistically 1–3 km in terrain despite the packaging. Fine around a neighbourhood.
• GMRS (US): a licence covers a whole family for ten years, allows more power and repeaters, and is the most practical family radio there.
• Amateur radio: needs a licence and an exam, and it is the only route to real capability — VHF/UHF handhelds give 1–5 km on the flat and 10–20 km from a hilltop, repeaters extend that while they have power, and HF reaches across a region or a continent.
• CB: licence-free in the US, common in vehicles, a few kilometres.
• Meshtastic / LoRa: licence-free, very low power, text only, typically 1–10 km per hop and more with height, self-forming mesh. Excellent for short household messages, and this app talks to it directly.
• Height beats power every time. Ten metres of elevation is worth more than ten watts.
§ The household plan
Write it on paper and give everyone a copy. It should survive every phone being dead.
• Two fixed check-in times, and what to do if somebody misses one.
• An out-of-area contact everyone calls or texts — local networks jam while long-distance links stay up.
• A primary meeting point and a fallback, and a time by which to act if nobody has been heard from.
• Where a written note gets left, so anyone arriving at an empty house knows where you went.
• Text rather than call: short messages get through congested networks that won't carry voice.
Runners and written notes cost nothing, emit nothing and don't need batteries. In a small community they are usually the right answer, and always the safe one.

guides.title: Security and OPSEC
guides.summary: Don't be worth robbing, don't be alone, and don't advertise. Light and noise discipline, layers, and neighbours.
guides.text:
Security is mostly avoidance. The household that nobody notices, that everyone on the street knows and likes, and that has nothing visibly worth taking, has already solved most of the problem. Everything below is about staying in that position.
§ Not being worth robbing
• Say nothing about what you have. Not to friends, not on the radio, not online, not to the neighbour who is only asking because he's frightened. The person known to be prepared becomes everybody else's plan.
• Rubbish is intelligence. Packaging tells anyone who looks exactly what you bought and how much of it. Burn or bury it away from the house.
• Keep the outside ordinary: no new lock glinting on a shabby door, no stack of jerrycans visible through a window, no smell of cooking meat at six o'clock when nobody else has any.
• Keep a working stock separate from your reserve, and let what's visible be modest.
§ Light and noise discipline
• One lit window on a dark street is visible for a kilometre and says the power, or the fuel, is here.
• Blackout material over windows before dark — hang it, tape it, and check it from outside. Use the lowest light that works; a dimmed red headlamp is enough to move around.
• Cook when other people cook, so smoke and smell aren't singular. Run a generator in daylight and only while it earns its fuel.
• At night, sound carries several times as far. Voices, a door slam, a dog, a chainsaw, an argument — all of it maps you.
§ Layers
Think in four: the neighbourhood, the boundary, the building, the room. Each layer should deter, delay and detect, and buy you time to decide.
• Neighbourhood: people who know your face and would knock if a stranger were at your door. Worth more than all the other layers combined.
• Boundary: gravel that crunches, a gate that squeaks, hedges low enough to see over, nothing to climb on, clear sightlines from a window.
• Building: most forced entries go through the door frame, not the lock. Long screws — 75 mm (3 in) — through the strike plate and hinges into the stud, plus a secondary bolt and a bar or wedge at night, do far more than an expensive cylinder. Film or a board on the vulnerable pane.
• Room: one room everybody can gather in, with a door that locks, a torch, a radio, and a way out.
§ Working with neighbours
• A street that co-operates is not a target, and a street that doesn't is a collection of individually vulnerable houses.
• Agree a signal — a whistle code, a phone tree, a light in a particular window — that means "come" or "trouble here".
• Share the load: a watch rota so everybody sleeps, one cooking fire instead of six, a list of who has skills, tools, a well, a generator, and who lives alone and needs checking.
• Take the vulnerable into the arrangement rather than around it. The people you help are the ones who will be awake at three in the morning when you need them.
§ If it goes wrong anyway
• Property is replaceable, and nothing in the house is worth a fight. Give it up, keep distance, break contact, withdraw to your gathering room, make noise, get help.
• Vary your routine — the time you fetch water, the route you take. Predictability is the vulnerability that most people never think about.
• Teach children what not to say, without frightening them: we don't talk about what's in our house.
• Keep documents, cash and copies somewhere separate from the obvious.
This is a defensive posture on purpose. Groups that start treating their neighbours as enemies get people killed, and become the thing they were afraid of.

guides.title: Barter and trade
guides.summary: Cash lasts longer than people think, skills trade better than goods, and never trade from your main stock.
guides.text:
Barter economies don't spring up the morning after. They grow out of favours between people who already know each other, and they arrive later than the films suggest. Plan for the sequence: cards fail, cash works, favours and sharing, then trade.
§ Money first
• Card networks and ATMs depend on power and connectivity; physical currency doesn't. Keep some cash at home in small denominations — nobody will have change, and a large note in a crisis buys you a small note's worth.
• Cash keeps working for weeks or months into most disruptions, and paying with it avoids every awkward negotiation below.
• Precious metals are poor short-term barter: hard to value, impossible to make change for, and an advertisement that you have more. They store value over years, not weeks.
§ What people actually want
Small, consumable, hard to make, immediately useful:
• Batteries (AA, AAA, 18650), lighters and matches, candles, cordage, tarpaulins, duct tape, fixings, tools and files.
• Soap, bleach, water treatment, toothpaste, sanitary supplies, nappies.
• Salt, sugar, coffee, tea, cooking oil, spices, yeast.
• Over-the-counter painkillers, antiseptic, dressings, reading glasses.
• Seed, fuel, hand-tools, sewing supplies, boot repair.
Alcohol, tobacco and ammunition trade extremely well and bring the wrong people to your door. Ammunition in particular may be pointed back at you. Decide in advance whether you want to be known as a source; it is very hard to become unknown afterwards.
§ Skills trade best
Nobody can steal a skill, it doesn't take up shelf space, and it renews. Welding, small-engine and bicycle repair, plumbing, sewing and shoe repair, butchery, food preservation, midwifery, dentistry, veterinary work, beekeeping, teaching children. Trade lessons as well as labour — the person who taught four neighbours to fix a bicycle is safer than the person who owns four bicycles.
§ Rules that keep you safe
• Never trade from your main stock. Keep a small, separate trading pool, and let it be all anyone sees.
• Trade in a neutral place, in daylight, with someone else present, and not at your front door. Never let a trading partner see your store or count your stock.
• With a new party, trade small first, and keep the second meeting somewhere else.
• Don't be the person known for having everything. Be one of several people who have some things.
• Value is local, volatile and personal — a bag of salt may be worthless in one street and priceless in the next. Don't stockpile "barter goods" as an investment; stockpile what you'd use yourself, and trade the surplus.
• Food you'll need in month six is not surplus in month two. Do the arithmetic before you feel generous.
§ Doing it properly at community scale
• A fixed market hour or day at a known place beats haggling door to door: fewer strangers wandering, more witnesses, better prices, less risk to everyone.
• A tool library, a labour exchange and a notice board move more value than any pile of trade goods.
• Keep written records of debts and promises, keep them simple, and expect to forgive some. Trying to enforce a debt in a community you depend on costs more than the debt.
• Generosity within a group you rely on is not charity, it is insurance. Trade with strangers; share with neighbours.

guides.title: Children, elderly and pets
guides.summary: The people and animals who can't compensate for a bad plan — and who show the effects of one first.
guides.text:
Fit adults absorb a lot of disorganisation. Children, the very old and animals do not: they dehydrate faster, get cold quicker, can't fetch their own water and can't tell you clearly what's wrong. They are also the reason most households cope, because looking after somebody is what keeps people functioning.
§ Children
• Routine and honesty. Keep wake times, meals and bedtime. Tell them what is true at a level they can hold — "the power is off, we have water and food, we're staying here tonight" — and don't let them overhear the adult version.
• Give them a job. A child with a task is less frightened. Fetching, sorting, counting stores, minding a younger one, keeping the log.
• Expect regression: bedwetting, clinginess, tantrums, nightmares, a six-year-old behaving like a three-year-old. It is normal, it passes, and punishing it makes it last longer.
• Play and lessons are not luxuries. They are how a child processes what's happening.
• Fluids: children dehydrate faster than adults. Watch urine — a nappy wet every 6 hours, an older child passing urine at least every 8. Oral rehydration solution at the first sign of diarrhoea, not on the third day.
• Infant feeding: keep breastfeeding if it is happening — protect the mother with food, fluid, rest and privacy rather than suggesting she stop. Powdered formula is not sterile: make it up with water boiled and cooled to about 70 °C, use within two hours, and never make a bottle in advance in warm conditions. Ready-to-feed liquid formula is the safer emergency option if you can get it.
• Hazards: candles, fuel cans, medication, generators, open water. Under-fives drown in 5 cm of water and are silent doing it.
• Put a card in each child's pocket with their name, your name and an out-of-area contact. Teach the meeting point until they can say it in their sleep.
§ Elderly
• Medication is the first crisis. A written list of every drug and dose, and a count of days remaining, on day one. Some drugs are dangerous to stop abruptly — see the medical guide.
• Cold and heat kill the old fastest. Indoor temperatures around 15 °C, sustained, cause hypothermia in frail people over days without anybody noticing it happening. Prioritise them for the warm room and the extra blanket.
• Thirst blunts with age, so schedule drinks rather than waiting for them to ask. Dehydration presents as confusion long before it presents as thirst.
• Sudden confusion in an older person is usually infection — very often a urinary infection — or dehydration, or a new drug. It is a symptom to investigate, not "just their age".
• Falls: clear the routes, keep a torch within reach of the bed, fix the loose rug, and think hard before rearranging furniture they navigate by habit.
• Spare glasses, hearing aid batteries, mobility aids, continence supplies, skin cream. Anyone bed-bound needs turning roughly every two hours to prevent pressure sores, which are agonising, get infected and take months to heal.
• Isolation and uselessness do real damage. Give them work they can do sitting down: mending, teaching, minding children, keeping records. Most of them have seen worse than you have.
§ Pets
• Water is the same problem as for people: roughly 50 ml per kg of body weight per day for a dog or a cat, more in heat.
• Store as many weeks of pet food as human food, plus a can opener, bowls and any medication. Cats are obligate carnivores and cannot live on grain and scraps.
• A carrier per animal, a lead, a muzzle for a frightened dog, litter and a plan for waste. Most emergency shelters won't take animals — know that before it becomes the reason you won't leave.
• Microchip details current, a tag with an out-of-area number, and a photo of you with the animal in case you're separated.
• Never feed dogs chocolate, onion, garlic, grapes, raisins or anything sweetened with xylitol.
• A dog is early warning, warmth and morale, and it also eats. Decide honestly what you can feed before the food runs low, not after.

guides.title: Morale and mental health
guides.summary: Morale is a logistics item. Sleep, structure, work and occasions — and the warning signs that need somebody to intervene.
guides.text:
More households come apart from exhaustion, boredom and resentment than from anything outside the door. Treat morale as a supply you have to produce daily, the same as water and heat.
§ Structure is the treatment
• Fixed wake time, three meals however small, work blocks, and a definite end to the day. Time that isn't shaped dissolves, and people who have lost the shape of a day stop washing, then stop eating, then stop trying.
• Ritual anchors: a hot drink at the same hour, one meal eaten together with everybody sitting down, clean clothes on a set day.
• Protect sleep above almost everything. Seven to eight hours, dark, quiet and warm. If there's a watch rota, rotate the bad shift so nobody gets broken sleep for days running — that is how good people start making dangerous mistakes.
• Get outdoors in the morning. Daylight early stabilises sleep, and physical work in daylight beats sitting with the radio on.
• Wash. Shave or don't, but decide. Standards are load-bearing.
§ What to expect, and what it means
In the first weeks most people get some of: hypervigilance, jumpiness, irritability, poor concentration, intrusive replays, vivid dreams, guilt about decisions, numbness, appetite loss. These are normal responses to abnormal events, not weakness and not illness. With sleep, food, safety and company, most of it fades.
The signs that need somebody to step in:
• Not eating or drinking, or not sleeping at all for several days.
• Withdrawing completely, or being unable to do the simplest task.
• Alcohol as the answer to every evening.
• Hopelessness, or talk of not being here.
Take talk of suicide seriously and ask directly — asking does not plant the idea, it usually brings relief. Don't leave the person alone, remove the obvious means, sit with them, and get them to anyone with more training than you have. Say plainly that you'll stay.
Alcohol deserves its own line: it wrecks sleep, dehydrates, dissolves judgement, and is the most common way a group takes a bad turn. Ration it deliberately or don't have it.
§ Running a group
• Brief people. Uncertainty is worse than bad news. A ten-minute meeting each morning: what we know, what changed, what we're doing today, who's doing it. Then everybody gets a job, including the ones who don't want one.
• Conflict is coming — over work, food, noise, somebody's partner, who gets the last of the coffee. Agree in advance how decisions get made and who has the final say, and deal with grievances early and in private. Small resentments break more groups than strangers do.
• Kindness and humour are force multipliers. So is one person who cooks properly with almost nothing.
• Praise the invisible work: water carried, waste dealt with, children kept calm.
§ Keeping hold of time
• Mark occasions — birthdays, Sundays, the solstice, the anniversary of something good. A calendar with things on it is how you know time is passing rather than dissolving.
• Have something to look forward to this week and something to look forward to next month.
• Keep entertainment that needs no power: cards, dice, books, an instrument, a chess set, someone who tells stories. It weighs nothing and it is genuinely the difference between a household that endures and one that grinds down.
• Name the losses out loud — people, plans, a version of the future you were entitled to expect. Grief that gets said is grief that moves.
